issues.legal_issue: The statutory reference to land does not exclude buildings from vesting when the legislation expressly includes them among the property acquired with a notified estate.
material_facts: A notification declared the estate vested in the State.
The disputed buildings stood on land within the notified estate.
The Act separately addressed buildings that vested on notification and buildings treated as settled with the intermediary.
issues.conclusion: The definition of an estate did not confine vesting to land; buildings falling within the statutory categories could also vest in the State.
issues.legal_principle: The definition of “estate” must be read with sections 4, 5 and 7 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950. Section 4(a) provides for vesting of specified buildings and other property, while sections 5 and 7 treat certain buildings as settled by the State with the intermediary, which presupposes that they first vested. No earlier cases were relied on.

rule.if: estate_vesting_proceeding and estate_vesting_notified and building_on_notified_estate and building_in_express_vesting_category

predicates.estate_vesting_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether property vested as part of an estate acquired by the State.
predicates.estate_vesting_notified: The State published a notification declaring the estate vested.
predicates.building_on_notified_estate: The building stood on land included in the notified estate.
predicates.building_in_express_vesting_category: The building fell within a category of buildings that the governing law expressly included in the property vesting with the estate.

issues.definition: When a notified estate includes a building in an expressly covered category, the building vests with the estate.

issues.legal_issue: For deciding whether a post-cutoff transfer of a rent-collection building may be annulled, the relevant use is its use immediately before the transfer, not its use after transfer or on the date of vesting.
material_facts: The owner leased the disputed properties to a company in 1947 and later transferred them to trustees in 1949.
The properties were said to have been used as a cutchery before the lease; the petitioners did not assert that they had not been used for rent collection before the relevant transfers.
The Collector issued a notice concerning the transfer, and the State alleged that the properties had been used as a cutchery before the lease.
issues.conclusion: Sections 4(a) and 4(h) must be read together: prior use as a rent-collection office or cutchery is relevant, and a qualifying post-cutoff transfer may be annulled after the prescribed inquiry and process, with the building then vesting in the State.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 4(a) and 4(h) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 must be read together. Under section 4(h), the Collector may inquire into a transfer made after the specified cutoff, and, if the stated improper purpose is established, may annul the transfer after notice and hearing and with prior State Government sanction. Reading the provisions to require rent-collection use after the transfer would defeat section 4(h), because the transferor would ordinarily cease using the building after transferring it. No earlier cases were relied on.

rule.if: estate_acquisition_proceeding and building_on_notified_estate and transfer_after_cutoff and building_used_for_rent_collection_before_transfer and transfer_made_to_defeat_acquisition_or_cause_state_loss_or_obtain_higher_compensation

predicates.estate_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns acquisition of an estate and the treatment of a building associated with it.
predicates.building_on_notified_estate: The building stood on land included in the estate acquired by the State.
predicates.transfer_after_cutoff: The proprietor transferred an interest in the building after the legally specified cutoff.
predicates.building_used_for_rent_collection_before: The proprietor used the building primarily as an office or cutchery to collect rent of the estate immediately before transferring it.
predicates.transfer_made_to_defeat_acquisition_or_c: The Collector found on inquiry that the transfer was made to defeat the acquisition law, cause loss to the State, or obtain higher compensation.

issues.definition: A post-cutoff transfer of a building on an acquired estate may be annulled, and the building may vest, when the building was used for rent collection before transfer and the transfer was made for a disallowed purpose.

issues.legal_issue: A challenge to the basis on which a notified estate vested is immaterial when vesting occurs under either applicable statutory route.
material_facts: The State published a notification declaring the owner's estate vested.
The petitioners argued that vesting occurred under the statutory provisions governing vesting rather than by virtue of the notification itself.
issues.conclusion: It was of little consequence whether the estate vested by publication of the notification or under the related vesting provisions, because vesting took place in either event.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the alternative statutory routes to vesting as immaterial to the result where vesting occurred under either route. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.estate_vesting_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether an estate vested in the State.
predicates.notification_declares_estate_vested: The State published a notification declaring that the estate vested.
predicates.law_provides_alternative_routes_to_vesti: The governing law provides more than one basis on which the estate may vest.

issues.definition: When a notification declares an estate vested and the law provides alternative routes to vesting, the estate vests regardless of which route applies.

issues.legal_issue: The provision permitting inquiry into and annulment of specified transfers does not impose an unconstitutional restriction when it forms part of a valid estate-acquisition law protected by the Constitution.
material_facts: The petitioners challenged the Collector's power to investigate and annul the transfer, arguing that the notice threatened their ability to receive rent and that no appeal or review was provided.
The provision required notice to and a hearing for affected parties, prior State Government sanction, and terms considered fair and equitable by the Collector.
The challenged power formed part of the machinery for acquiring estates under the Act.
issues.conclusion: The challenge failed: the Collector's power was not as absolute or arbitrary as alleged, and the Act, including the challenged provision, was protected by Article 31-A of the Constitution.
issues.legal_principle: The Court considered the safeguards requiring notice, hearing and prior State Government sanction, as well as the provision's role as an integral part of a valid law for acquisition of estates. It held that the Act, including section 4(h) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, was protected by Article 31-A of the Constitution. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_estate_acqui: A party challenges the constitutionality of a law used to acquire estates.
predicates.annulment_power_is_integral_to_acquisiti: The power to review and annul specified transfers forms part of the machinery for acquiring estates.
predicates.affected_parties_receive_notice_and_hear: The decision-maker must give affected parties notice and an opportunity to be heard before annulling a transfer.
predicates.government_approval_is_required: The decision-maker must obtain the government's prior approval before annulling a transfer.
predicates.acquisition_law_is_constitutionally_prot: The governing law for acquiring estates is protected by the Constitution from the asserted fundamental-rights challenge.

issues.definition: A constitutional challenge fails when the challenged power is integral to estate acquisition, procedural safeguards apply, and the acquisition law is constitutionally protected.
